n: The Lord appears to Abraham by the trees of Mamre as he sits at his tent door during the hottest part of the day, a time when travelers would normally rest.

f.g: Better “the oaks of Mamre,” near Hebron.

n: Abraham sees three men and runs—at ninety-nine, in the heat—to welcome them, bowing low. His eager hospitality is a model of kindness to strangers.

f.g: The JST describes them as holy men sent from God; one speaks for the Lord.

n: Abraham begs his guests to stay and let him serve them. He calls himself their servant—humility and hospitality go together.

f.g: The JST reads “My brethren.” The Hebrew can be a respectful “my lord” or the divine title.

n: He offers water to wash their dusty feet and shade to rest under—basic courtesies in a hot, dry land.
Abraham modestly offers “a morsel of bread,” then provides a feast. The visitors accept.

f.g: Refresh yourselves; strengthen your hearts with food.

n: Abraham hurries to Sarah, asking her to bake a large quantity of fresh bread from the finest flour.

f.g: About 20 quarts (22 liters) of flour—far more than three guests could eat; generous hospitality.
Round flatbreads baked on hot stones.

n: He runs to choose a tender calf for a servant to prepare. Meat was a rare luxury, reserved for honored guests.

f.g: Prepare; cook.

n: Abraham serves curds, milk, and meat, and stands nearby like a servant while they eat under the tree.

f.g: Probably curds or yogurt.

n: The visitors ask for Sarah by name—a surprising detail, since strangers would not know it. Their visit is about her.

f.g: Their knowledge of Sarah’s new name hints that they are no ordinary travelers.

n: The speaker promises to return the next year, when Sarah will have a son. Sarah, listening behind the tent door, overhears.

f.w: according to the time of life
f.g: “When the season comes around”—about this time next year.

n: The narrator explains that Sarah was long past childbearing age. Only a miracle could fulfill this promise.

f.g: Very advanced in years.

f.w: it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women
f.g: She had gone through menopause.

n: Sarah laughs to herself at the idea. Her laugh is understandable—she has waited decades, and now the promise sounds impossible.

f.g: Another wordplay on Isaac’s name, “he laughs.”
Grown old.

n: The Lord knows Sarah’s silent thoughts and asks why she laughed. Nothing is hidden from Him.

f.g: Why.

n: Here is one of the great questions of scripture: “Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” The answer, shown in Isaac’s birth, is no.

f.w: Is any thing too hard for the LORD?

n: Frightened, Sarah denies laughing. The Lord gently but firmly corrects her. He does not reject her—He simply invites honesty.

f.g: Sarah’s fear is natural; later she laughs again—this time with joy (21:6).

n: The visitors set out toward Sodom, and Abraham walks with them to see them off, as a good host would.

f.w: to bring them on the way
f.g: To escort them part of the way.

n: The Lord considers whether to share His plans with Abraham. God treats Abraham as a trusted friend.
Because Abraham will be a great nation and a blessing to all peoples, God wants him to understand His ways of justice and mercy.

f.w: all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him

n: God has chosen Abraham so he will teach his children and household to follow the Lord’s ways. Parents teaching righteousness is part of how God’s promises are fulfilled.

f.g: Righteousness and justice—doing what is right and fair.

n: An outcry has risen against Sodom and Gomorrah—perhaps the cries of their victims. Their sin is very serious.

f.g: Hebrew zeʿaqah — often the cry of the oppressed for help.

n: Like a just judge, the Lord will examine the facts before judging.

f.w: I will go down now, and see

n: Two of the men head for Sodom while Abraham remains standing before the Lord—ready to intercede.

f.g: In chapter 19 these two are called angels.

n: Abraham steps forward and boldly asks whether God will destroy the righteous along with the wicked.

f.g: To come near—language used of approaching God in prayer and worship.

n: Abraham suggests fifty righteous people. Lot and his family are surely on his mind.

f.g: Perhaps; suppose.

n: Abraham appeals to God’s own character: surely the Judge of all the earth will act justly. He prays not to change God, but in harmony with what he knows of God.

f.w: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?

n: God agrees: for fifty righteous people He will spare the whole city. A few righteous can protect many.
Abraham humbly acknowledges he is only “dust and ashes,” yet continues to plead. Humility and boldness can go together in prayer.

f.g: A phrase of deep humility; mortal and lowly.

n: Abraham asks whether five fewer would matter. God agrees to spare it for forty-five.

f.g: Forty-five.

n: Abraham presses on to forty, and God agrees again.

f.g: For the sake of forty people.

n: Abraham, careful not to presume, asks about thirty. God again agrees.

f.w: Oh let not the Lord be angry
f.g: A respectful plea not to offend God by persistence.

n: Abraham dares to ask about twenty, and God agrees.

f.g: I have dared; I have ventured.

n: Abraham’s final request is for ten, and God agrees. The tragedy is that not even ten will be found.

f.g: Some Jewish tradition later saw ten as the minimum for a community.

n: The Lord departs, and Abraham returns home. His intercession shows the heart of a covenant person who cares for others’ salvation.

f.g: Talking intimately; conversing.
